us-house.budget-law-enforcement: a budget law providing extra money, about 0.6 percent of a year's economic output, for border barriers and immigration enforcement, mainly over four years; it lifts annual funding for immigration detention roughly fourfold and introduces fees on asylum claims, on asylum seekers' permits to work, and on temporary protection from removal
us-house.detention-mandate-law: a law that makes immigration authorities detain any resident lacking legal status who has been charged, though not convicted, with theft, burglary, shoplifting, or assault on a police officer. By the immigration authorities' own estimate, the first year costs about 0.1 percent of a year's economic output
us-house.enforcement-funding-law: a budget law providing extra money for immigration enforcement, about 0.23 percent of a year's economic output across about three years, mainly for enforcement operations and for hiring more enforcement officers
us-house.protected-status-bill: a bill that would make the government extend by three years the temporary shield from removal, including work permits, held by about 350,000 people from a single country, about 0.1 percent of the population, after the government had acted to end it

uk-commons.work-visa-rules: changes to the rules ending overseas recruitment of care workers on work visas and lifting the skill level for other work visas to degree level. The government expected work visas to fall by about 12,000 to 15,000 a year, about 0.02 percent of the population
uk-commons.asylum-bill: a bill narrowing family and private-life claims in immigration cases, folding refugee status and humanitarian protection into a single status and setting when it may be withdrawn, and requiring asylum seekers to pay back support when able. The government expected about 14,000 more refusals a year of requests to stay on family or private-life grounds, about 0.02 percent of the population
uk-commons.settlement-wait-decision: a decision lengthening the standard wait before migrants may settle permanently from five years to ten, setting waits of at least twenty years for refugees on the main protection route and for those who used public benefits, and cutting the wait for high earners. The government expected more than 500,000 people, about 0.7 percent of the population, to become eligible to settle later over five years than under the old rules

de-bundestag.family-reunification-suspension: a law that pauses family reunification for two years for people with subsidiary protection, except in hardship cases; it had allowed about 12,000 visas a year, about 0.01 percent of the population

fr-assemblee.territory-birthright-law: a law requiring, before a child born to foreign parents in one overseas territory can become a citizen, that both parents and not just one had legal residence in the country for at least a year, instead of three months, when the child was born. About 1,577 minors a year, about 0.002 percent of the population, had become citizens under the previous rule
fr-assemblee.detention-210-law: a law that extends the longest immigration detention from 90 to 210 days for foreigners facing removal orders who are considered a particularly serious threat to public order

ca-commons.levels-plan: a three-year plan for immigration that fixes new temporary residents next year at about 0.9 percent of the population, a target 43 percent lower than the year before, and holds new permanent residents at about 0.9 percent of the population each year, a target about 4 percent lower than the year before
ca-commons.borders-act: a law denying a hearing to asylum claims filed more than a year after first entry, or more than 14 days after a crossing of the land border between official crossings, and empowering the government to cancel, suspend, or stop processing whole groups of immigration documents and applications
ca-commons.citizenship-descent-law: a law granting citizenship by descent to children born abroad beyond the first generation where the citizen parent had lived in the country for at least three years in total before the birth, and restoring it to those excluded by the previous one-generation cap. Official estimates put the number affected between tens of thousands and about 115,000, up to about 0.3 percent of the population
ca-commons.permanent-residence-measure: a one-off step in next year's immigration plan offering permanent residence to as many as 200,000 temporary residents already living in the country, about 0.5 percent of the population, with yearly targets left as they were
